page: Vultr vc2-8c-32gb is a General Purpose virtual machine belonging to the Cloud Compute family. It features an Intel x86_64 processor with 8 shared vCPUs, mapped from 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The system is configured with 32.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Storage is bundled as a local 640 GB NVMe SSD, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. No GPU accelerators are present.

Benchmark evaluations indicate a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core performance. Single-core metrics, such as stress-ng single-core CPU and Geekbench single-core tests, fall into the bottom 10% tier. However, multi-core performance scales to average levels, as demonstrated by stress-ng multi-core and Passmark CPU scores. Memory read bandwidth remains average for both small and large blocks, though large-block memory write bandwidth is limited, placing in the bottom 10%. Computational tasks like software compilation with Clang and ray tracing achieve average throughput, while database operations and static web serving throughput register in the bottom 25%.

The shared CPU allocation introduces potential resource contention, which explains the lower single-core performance and makes it less suitable for latency-sensitive workloads. Qualitatively, the server offers a cost-effective resource density for multi-threaded applications that can leverage the 8 vCPUs and 32.0 GB of RAM without requiring dedicated CPU guarantees. Best-fit workloads include multi-threaded background processing, development environments, moderate web serving, and basic container orchestration.

Operating on a shared CPU architecture with 4 physical cores and hyper-threading, this instance exhibits a performance profile characterized by weak single-core execution but average multi-core processing capabilities. While memory read bandwidth is average, memory write speeds and database operations fall into lower performance tiers. The shared CPU model offers a cost-effective option for resource-dense workloads that do not require dedicated CPU guarantees. It is best suited for multi-threaded background tasks, software compilation, and general-purpose staging environments.
